title: People really hate AI, so why can’t they get enough?
key_facts: A first-person commentary: the author says a love/hate attitude toward AI is common around the world.

Pew Research Center: more US adults think AI will have a negative impact on them personally and on society than expect a positive one, with pessimism strongest among the young; a Stanford report says more than half of people worldwide say AI products make them nervous.
Gallup poll in May: 71% of US adults would oppose a new AI data centre in their area, against 53% who would oppose a new nuclear power plant; an NBC poll in March found AI less popular than ICE.
Sensor Tower: ChatGPT reached a billion monthly users in May and Google DeepMind's Gemini 950 million in July.

Pew: half of US adults say they use a chatbot, more than twice the 2023 share, and one in four use one every day; more than a third of adults in all 38 OECD countries used generative AI in the last three months.

The author's explanation: when people say they hate AI it is the companies' relentless push to put the technology everywhere, and their warnings of the biggest upheaval in generations, that they dislike, not the technology.

The author notes that, unlike with social media, there is still a chance for public influence: all 50 US states have passed or proposed AI laws (more than 2,100 bills, a tenfold rise in three years) and open-source alternatives exist.
The author concedes that trillion-dollar companies are hard to move.
quote_evidence: But here’s what I really think is going on: When people say they hate AI it’s not the technology they dislike but, rather, the relentless drive of the companies behind it to push the tech upon us in as many ways as possible.
ChatGPT hit a billion monthly users in May, according to the market analysis firm Sensor Tower.
In a Gallup poll in May, 71% of US adults said they would oppose construction of a new AI data center in their area, far more than the 53% who said they would oppose a new nuclear power plant.
why_it_matters_hint: The piece argues that public anger at AI is directed at the companies' push, which may leave room for regulation and consumer choice.
notes: Read in full. Opinion and analysis in the first person; the author's name is not in the fetched text. Polls cited (Pew, Stanford, Gallup May, NBC March, Sensor Tower) are quoted as the commentary reports them and were not checked against their sources. Analysis is kept apart from facts by naming the piece a commentary.
